edges.description: Inappropriate insulin secretion produces the defining hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia phenotype.

Severe neuroglycopenia from hypoglycemia can present with generalized seizures.
Delayed diagnosis or recurrent hypoglycemia can cause neurologic damage and developmental delay.
intermediate_mechanisms: Recurrent or delayed-treated hypoglycemia injures the developing brain.

nodes.description: Monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by SLC16A1) is normally silenced in the beta cell, which is what keeps circulating pyruvate and lactate from acting as insulin secretagogues. Promoter variants that de-repress SLC16A1 transcription in the beta cell let pyruvate enter, be oxidized, and stimulate insulin release. The transporter activity is increased in the beta cell because the protein is expressed there ectopically, not because the encoded transporter is more active. Because the trigger is an exogenous monocarboxylate rather than glucose, hypoglycemia appears after anaerobic exercise or a pyruvate load rather than on fasting.

evidence.reference_title: Physical exercise-induced hypoglycemia caused by failed silencing of monocarboxylate transporter 1 in pancreatic beta cells.
evidence.snippet: These studies show that promoter-activating mutations in EIHI induce SLC16A1 expression in beta cells, where this gene is not usually transcribed, permitting pyruvate uptake and pyruvate-stimulated insulin release despite ensuing hypoglycemia.

molecular_functions: MCT1 proton-coupled monocarboxylate symporter activity (ectopic in beta cells)

nodes.description: Activating variants in GCK, the beta-cell glucose sensor, raise glucokinase catalytic efficiency and lower its glucose half-saturation concentration. Because glucokinase sets the glucose concentration at which glycolytic flux begins to raise the beta-cell ATP/ADP ratio, the whole secretory system is recalibrated downwards: insulin is released at plasma glucose levels that would normally silence it. The channel itself is intact, which is why this arm converges on the same depolarization node rather than replacing it.

nodes.description: In a distinct mechanistic arm, dominant activating GLUD1 variants (hyperinsulinism-hyperammonemia syndrome) or recessive HADH/SCHAD deficiency increase glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) activity in the beta cell. Leucine allosterically activates GDH, driving glutamate oxidation through the TCA cycle, raising the ATP/ADP ratio, and converging on the same K-ATP-channel closure and insulin-release pathway, producing protein/leucine-sensitive hypoglycemia. Increased GDH activity in liver/kidney also generates the mild hyperammonemia characteristic of HI/HA syndrome.

nodes.description: Inappropriate insulin secretion produces severe, often non-ketotic hypoglycemia. Because insulin suppresses ketogenesis, the brain is deprived of both glucose and the ketone bodies it would normally use as an alternative fuel during fasting, so neuroglycopenia is more profound than in other causes of hypoglycemia. Recurrent or prolonged hypoglycemia carries a considerable risk of seizures, developmental delay, and permanent neurological damage.

nodes.description: Inactivating variants in ABCC8 (SUR1) or KCNJ11 (Kir6.2), which together form the beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channel, cause loss of channel expression or function. The K-ATP channel is the central regulator of insulin secretion: under normal conditions it keeps the beta-cell membrane hyperpolarized when glucose is low. Loss of K-ATP channel function removes this brake on the membrane potential. K-ATP channel defects are the most common molecular cause of CHI and underlie both diffuse and focal histological disease.

nodes.description: The downstream consequence of K-ATP channel loss of function (or of amino-acid/metabolic defects upstream of the channel) is constitutive beta-cell membrane depolarization, opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, increased cytosolic calcium, and exocytosis of insulin granules. The result is inappropriate insulin secretion that continues despite hypoglycemia, the biochemical hallmark of CHI.
